Darwin Lake comes into view after the climb above Tagus Cove on Isabela Island. Its water lies within a volcanic cone, surrounded by dry slopes and low vegetation. From above, the shape of the lake is easy to see: its enclosed basin contrasts sharply with the open ocean on the other side of the shore.

The lake is saline, although it looks like an ordinary island lake. This makes it an intriguing stop for anyone who likes asking questions about the natural world. A guide's explanations help connect the water, volcanic rock and the history of how this coastline formed. Small birds can be spotted during the climb, making it pleasant to pause and watch them.

It's worth lingering beside the lake to watch clouds and patches of sunlight change the color of the water. Then turn toward the cove and compare two very different landscapes on the same island. This spot will appeal to those who enjoy short uphill walks and sweeping views. Darwin Lake on Isabela is easily distinguished from Darwin Bay on Genovesa: it is a separate inland body of water reached from Tagus Cove.

## The City of David

With the feel of a small provincial town, David is Panama's second-largest city.

## David — a Starting Point for Travel Routes!

Many travel routes begin here. The city's favorable location has attracted substantial foreign investment, helping David grow rapidly while it strives to preserve its historical heritage. The city can broadly be divided into old and new districts. David has everything needed for an enjoyable stay, from cafés and restaurants to discos and nightclubs. Visitors come away with fond memories of their time in the city.

Deception Island is part of the South Shetland Islands near the Antarctic Peninsula. Its harbor, Port Foster, occupies the flooded caldera of an active volcano. A ring of dark slopes and glaciers surrounds the inner waters, while a narrow passage known as Neptune's Bellows connects them to the open sea.

Volcanic ash gives the shore its dark color, and geothermal heat warms parts of the beaches. The island has historic monuments and protected natural areas with their own rules for visitors. The expedition team chooses the specific bay and decides whether a landing is possible according to the weather, sea conditions and conservation requirements.

Venezuela, a country rich in attractions, invites you to discover the Orinoco River Delta! Its waters rush down from the foothills of the Andes, forming one of the country's most beautiful regions. Here you can see tropical forests and mangrove thickets. Differences in the color and composition of the water, as well as the local ecosystems, divide the waterways into "white" and "black" channels. There are almost no mosquitoes around the "black rivers," and caimans do not live in their waters. The "white" rivers, by contrast, teem with wildlife and insects.

This is the land of the Warao people, who live along the rivers; it is their ancestral home. They fish, hunt and practice traditional crafts, and you can buy the things they make. As you travel by boat through the Orinoco Delta, you may hope to encounter the world-famous anaconda, capybaras and enormous crocodiles! If you continue farther by boat, you will reach Canaima National Park. The Guiana Massif, where the reserve is located, is among the planet's oldest places, with an age of approximately 2 million years.

The landscape of Canaima National Park evokes the lost world described in Arthur Conan Doyle's books, and many adventure films have been shot here. Within the reserve is a beautiful lake, with an old town on its shore.

Another remarkable natural phenomenon here is the tepui, the name Indigenous people give to these mountains. They resemble truncated pyramids with flat summits, where traces of various plant and animal species from ancient times have been preserved. And of course there is Angel Falls (1,054 m high), its rainbow-colored streams plunging from a tremendous height. Incidentally, the waterfall is named after the American pilot who first discovered this natural wonder. There are also the jewel-like Sapo and Yuri waterfalls. You can reach Orchid Island by boat as well. You will no longer find orchids there, but its unusually pinkish sand, flawlessly blue water and surrounding palms are a delight.
